newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish rulers welcome Pope's political restraint.
newsitem.headline: Polish rulers welcome Pope's political restraint.

text.p: Pope John Paul has inspired Poland's Roman Catholics at a time when his native country is riven by political rows over the role of the Church.

But the ruling ex-communists, confronting the Polish bishops and the pro-Catholic right four months before general elections, are clearly relieved that he has not gone further in suggesting how he would like Poles to vote.

"I expressed my...gratitude to the Pope for the fact that there is an atmosphere of calm, which we need so much, during his pilgrimage," Prime Minister Wlodzimerz Cimoszewicz, a former communist, said after meeting the Pontiff on Sunday.
The Pope told Poland's bishops that such areas as advancing political thought should be left to lay people to pursue in keeping with Christian teaching.
"They (laity) certainly must be helped in this task, but no-one should take their place," he said in a message on Sunday to the bishops.
But once the Pope returns to the Vatican on Tuesday the rows between politicians -- dampened out of respect for his presence -- are likely to resume.

"There is a danger the Pope's visit will be politicised, because politicians seize every chance to achieve their goals,", Tadeusz Pieronek, general secretary of the Polish bishops conference, said at a news conference.

The head of the biggest opposition group, the trade-union led Solidarity Election Action (AWS), hopes the visit will prompt a "moral awakening" that spells defeat for the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD).
Solidarity's Marian Krzaklewski, who was blessed by the Pope at a mass on Friday, told reporters the Pontiff had urged him to "hold fast".
The polls due in September may show whether Krzaklewski's hopes bear fruit in a country where 90 percent of the people are Catholics but have mixed views about the Church.
During his trip the Pope condemned abortion, now effectively legal in Poland under a 1996 reform backed by the secular-minded left in the face of Church-led opposition.
The abortion issue is now deadlocked after a constitutional court last month challenged the liberalised law, and the ex-communists have called for a referendum to settle it.

The Church opposes this idea and Bishop Pieronek said one of the first fruits of the Pope's visit was the fact that ex-communist President Aleksander Kwasniewski and a leftist opposition party had rejected a referendum on abortion.
"Certain slight changes can be noted already. For example, that President Kwasniewski and the Labour Union (UP) no longer insist that a referendum should be staged," Pieronek said.

The Pope has insisted crucifixes should stay on the walls of schoolrooms and public offices where they were hung after the 1989 fall of communism, despite arguments that they infringe the principle of separating Church and state.
The Pontiff has also sprung to the defence of the conservative Polish Church against attacks by its critics.
"Saying that the Church is an enemy of freedom makes no sense, especially here in Poland," the Pope said, recalling its defence of human rights under communism.
The Church is indeed fiercely attacked by anti-clerical voices, mainly from within the social democratic party rooted in the communist system that once persecuted the Church.

But criticisms of Polish bishops, some of whom have denounced Poland's rulers for their Marxist roots or speak of alleged conspiracies against the country by freemasons, is also voiced by some lay Catholics and even theologians and priests.

Centrist and leftist opposition politicians were dismayed last month when the Church reversed its pledge of neutrality and criticised a new compromise Polish constitution they had helped to draft, just before it was passed in a referendum.
